text:
A 2026 systematic review brought together 22 randomised trials, involving 2,567 participants, of psychological approaches designed specifically to reduce loneliness. The most consistent evidence was for cognitive behavioural approaches, which were associated with reductions in loneliness. These programs helped people reappraise unhelpful thoughts about loneliness, ease avoidance, build coping skills and engage socially.

Why this matters across roles: loneliness can arise even when someone is not socially isolated. The authors note that psychological barriers may stop people using the social opportunities around them. So it helps to look at how a person thinks about connection, not only how much contact they have.

One practical takeaway for any role: listen for beliefs about connection, such as "people do not really want me there." Reflect them back gently rather than arguing. Asking "What tends to stop you reaching out?" can open a useful conversation. If loneliness is long standing, sits alongside low mood or is affecting daily life, talk with the person about involving their GP or a psychologist.

Where the evidence stops:
• Every trial was judged to carry some or high risk of bias, and many were small with short follow up.
• The review covered psychological approaches only, so it does not settle whether these do better than increasing social contact.
• No included study assessed cost effectiveness.

Key source: Birken et al., 2026: https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03639-3
